title: Intel Stock Has Moved an Average of 16% the Day After Its Last 3 Reports. Should You Buy Before the Next One?
detail:
Intel Stock Has Moved an Average of 16% the Day After Its Last 3 Reports. Should You Buy Before the Next One?
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 12:37 PM MST 5 min read
INTC
NVDA

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) is set to post its third-quarter results after the closing bell on Thursday, Oct. 29. And lately, the trading session after an Intel report has been wild.

The stock dropped 17% the day after Intel's January report, surged 24% after April's, and fell 8% after July's. These three moves average about 16% in one session.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

With shares near $93 as I write, a move that size would mean about $15 a share up or down.

But the quarter Intel had just finished didn't set the direction. The company topped its own financial forecast all three times, and the stock still dropped twice. I think what management said about the coming months mattered more every time.

Image source: Intel.

January and April

In January, Intel posted fourth-quarter 2025 revenue of $13.7 billion and $0.15 in non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share, both above the company's own outlook. But management forecast first-quarter 2026 revenue between $11.7 billion and $12.7 billion, with break-even adjusted earnings per share. The midpoint of that revenue range was around 11% under the fourth quarter's total.

"We expect our available supply to be at its lowest level in Q1 before improving in Q2 and beyond," CFO David Zinsner said in the January earnings release.

Shares dropped 17% the next day.

Three months later, the outlook pointed up. Intel's first-quarter revenue of $13.6 billion was $1.4 billion over the midpoint of its forecast. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.29 also beat the break-even level management had guided for, but Zinsner said around 6 cents of that came from a one-time gain.

What's more, Intel forecast second-quarter revenue of $13.8 billion to $14.8 billion, up 2% to 9% over the first quarter. The stock surged 24% on April 24 -- its best day since 1987.

Why did the stock fall in July?

July's report was arguably the best of the three. Second-quarter revenue of $16.1 billion was up 25% from the year before and $1.8 billion above the midpoint of Intel's forecast. Revenue in its data center and AI segment jumped 59% year over year. Adjusted earnings per share landed at $0.42, more than twice the $0.20 management had guided for.

Yet the third-quarter forecast looked flatter. Its revenue midpoint of $16.3 billion sat only about 1% above the second quarter, and Intel guided for adjusted earnings per share of $0.38, down from $0.42. Intel also lifted its 2026 capital spending outlook to over $20 billion, which Zinsner said was "up significantly versus our expectations entering the year."

title: Why Comfort Systems Plunged Today
detail:
Why Comfort Systems Plunged Today
Billy Duberstein, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 12:39 PM MST 3 min read
FIX
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of Comfort Systems (NYSE:FIX) fell as much as 13.2% on Friday, before recovering to an 8.9% decline at 3:10 p.m. EDT.

Comfort Systems reported earnings last night, handily beating revenue and earnings estimates. However, the company also announced that one of the company's founders and longtime Chief Financial Officer, Bill George, will retire at the end of the year.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

During this earnings season, even good results are leading to stock declines for most companies levered to the AI build-out. Therefore, the retirement announcement, combined with a "sell the news" mentality, appears to be the cause of today's sell-off.

Comfort Systems continues to thrive

Comfort Systems has been a massive winner due to the AI data center build-out, given its expertise in the cooling, plumbing, ventilation, and electrical systems that AI data centers require.

Third-quarter results continued that trend, with revenue growing a whopping 53.7% and earnings per share growing an even higher 68.6% to $13.91. Both figures beat analyst expectations by a fair amount.

Not only were current results terrific, but the company's backlog grew to $17.8 billion from $14.1 billion just three months prior. That's a 26.2% quarter-over-quarter growth rate in the backlog, which would amount to a 153.7% annualized rate.

This makes Comfort Systems' sell-off all the more confusing today. However, there have been many similar sell-offs this week in AI stocks, with blockbuster earnings often met with selling pressure. It appears some investors may be anticipating the end of the AI build-out next year, even as tech executives say the opposite.

Image source: Getty Images.

Comfort Systems is reasonably priced now

Comfort Systems is now about 38% off its all-time high set back in June, while shares trade at 19.4 times the average 2027 analyst earnings estimate.

That's a very reasonable valuation for Comfort Systems if the AI build-out continues beyond 2027. However, doubts over that prospect, along with the CFO's retirement announcement, appear to be dominating sentiment today.

title: Prediction: Here's What a $5,000 Investment in Rivian Will Be Worth in 5 Years

Prediction: Here's What a $5,000 Investment in Rivian Will Be Worth in 5 Years
Jeff Siegel, The Motley Fool

RIVN
NVDA
TSLA

Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ: RIVN) trades around $12 per share, giving the electric vehicle manufacturer a market capitalization of about $18 billion. That's a fraction of Tesla's valuation, but Rivian still has a long way to go before achieving consistent profitability.

Still, with production accelerating and its lower-priced R2 SUV now reaching customers, Rivian could look a lot different five years from now. My prediction? A $5,000 investment today could be worth approximately $10,000 by 2031.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The R2 could transform Rivian's business

Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter, up about 45% year over year. Management also reaffirmed its full-year delivery guidance of 65,000 to 70,000 vehicles. Worth noting: much of Rivian's future growth depends on the R2.

Unlike Rivian's more expensive R1 SUV, the R2 is designed to appeal to a much broader market. Initial versions start around $58,000, with a lower-priced standard version clocking in at $45,000 in 2027. Higher production volumes should also help Rivian spread its manufacturing costs across more vehicles, potentially improving profitability. But Rivian's ambitions extend beyond selling electric vehicles, too.

Image source: Getty Images.

The company recently landed a deal with Uber Technologies involving an initial 10,000 autonomous R2 vehicles, with an option for another 40,000. Uber also agreed to invest up to $1.25 billion in Rivian through 2031, contingent on certain milestones.

Rivian's existing software business has been growing, too. The segment generated $515 million in Q2 revenue, with a gross margin of 42%. Its partnership with Volkswagen also provides another avenue to monetize vehicle software and electrical architecture.

What could $5,000 become?

Rivian shares closed at $12.34 on Oct. 19. At that price, a $5,000 investment would purchase approximately 405 shares. My five-year target is $25 per share. Here's how I arrive at that number.

The EV maker should be able to grow annual deliveries to 250,000 vehicles by 2031. This is a reasonable target considering the company's manufacturing expansion, which should push combined annual production capacity to 515,000 vehicles across its Illinois and Georgia facilities. Assuming an average selling price of $50,000, those deliveries would generate approximately $12.5 billion in automotive revenue.

title: Robinhood Is Quietly Building 13 Businesses at Once. Here's Why It Matters.
detail:
Robinhood Is Quietly Building 13 Businesses at Once. Here's Why It Matters.
Lawrence Nga, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 12:05 PM MST 5 min read
HOOD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ: HOOD) started with a simple idea: Make it easier for ordinary people to invest.

That sounds like a single business. But it isn't anymore. By the second quarter of 2026, Robinhood had 13 business lines generating at least $100 million of annualized revenue. That's up from just one in 2019 and nine in 2024.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

At first, this might look like another impressive growth statistic. But digging deeper, I think it tells us something more important -- that Robinhood is getting better at turning one customer relationship into multiple sources of revenue.

Image source: Getty Images.
From one business to many

Robinhood originally built its business around stock trading. But it didn't stop there. It kept adding products. Options became an important revenue stream. Crypto followed. Robinhood added margin lending, cash products, Gold membership subscriptions, securities lending, prediction markets, credit cards, etc. Each product gave Robinhood another way to make money from its customers.

That's an important strategy. A traditional broker might make money when a customer trades. Robinhood increasingly has opportunities to make money, whether that customer is trading, holding cash, paying for a subscription, using a card, borrowing against securities, or participating in other financial products.

The company doesn't need every product to become enormous. It needs enough of them to become meaningful. So far, that's happening.

The customer matters more than the product

This is where Robinhood's strategy is particularly important.

Imagine someone opens a Robinhood account to buy a few stocks. That customer might initially generate very little revenue. But over time, Robinhood can offer more products. The customer could subscribe to its Gold membership. Move more cash onto the platform. Trade options. Use the Gold Card. Buy crypto. Participate in prediction markets, and more. The customer doesn't need to find another financial company for each activity.

As for Robinhood, it can continue to expand the relationship, generating more revenue over time. Better still, it doesn't have to spend on customer acquisition costs, making growth highly efficient over time.

A few numbers show how customers are becoming more valuable. Robinhood ended the second quarter with 28.4 million funded customers, up 7% from a year earlier. Gold subscribers reached 4.8 million, up 39%, while average revenue per user increased 24% to $187.
